translation: My food is to do the will of the one who sent me and to finish his work.
notes: The sentence employs a metaphorical definition where 'food' (βρῶμα) is equated not to physical sustenance but to spiritual obedience and mission fulfillment. The structure relies on two infinitive clauses introduced by the conjunction 'ἵνα' (ina) which functions here as a noun clause (equivalent to 'to do' and 'to finish') serving as the predicate nominative complement to 'is' (ἐστί). The verb 'τελειώσω' (to finish/perfect) carries a nuance of bringing something to its intended completion or maturity, reflecting the theological concept of fulfilling a divine purpose. The use of 'ὁ πέμψαντός με' (the one who sent me) utilizes a perfect participle in the genitive case to denote the agent, emphasizing the authority and prior action of the sender. The sentence exhibits a parallel structure (asyndeton within the coordinated clauses) between 'to do the will' and 'to finish the work,' reinforcing the unity of the speaker's mission.

translation: Do you not say that it is still four months until the harvest comes?
notes: The sentence employs a rhetorical question structure, introduced by the negative particle οὐχ (oukh) combined with the present indicative λέγετε (legete), to challenge a common assumption or statement of fact held by the listeners. The adverb ἔτι (eti) meaning 'still' modifies the temporal phrase τετράμηνος (tetramēnos), emphasizing the perceived duration of the wait. The construction οὐχ ὑμεῖς λέγετε οὗτι... ('Do you not say that...') functions as an idiomatic way to introduce a shared belief that the speaker intends to reinterpret or transcend. The sentence contrasts the literal agricultural timeline of 'four months' with the immediacy of the coming 'harvest' (θερισμός), which in this context serves as a metaphor for spiritual readiness or judgment. The syntax presents two coordinated clauses within the reported speech: 'it is still four months' and 'the harvest comes,' linked by καί (kai), highlighting the discrepancy between the expected waiting period and the actual arrival of the event.

translation: Behold, I say to you, lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are white for harvest.
notes: The sentence opens with the imperative particle 'ἰδού' (behold/look), which serves as a discourse marker to draw immediate attention to the following instruction. The main verb 'λέγω' (I say) is in the present indicative, functioning as an emphatic assertion often found in the Synoptic Gospels and Johannine literature. The commands 'ἐπάρατε' (lift up) and 'θεάσασθε' (look/behold) are both in the aorist imperative, second person plural, indicating a sudden, decisive action required of the listeners. The syntax employs a clear asyndetic connection between the two imperatives linked by 'καί', creating a rhythmic, urgent sequence. The clause introduced by 'ὅτι' (for/because) provides the theological rationale for the action: the fields are 'λευκαί' (white). In this agricultural metaphor, 'white' signifies that the grain is fully ripe and ready for gathering, a common image in Jewish and early Christian literature symbolizing the urgency of the spiritual harvest. The preposition 'πρός' with the accusative 'θερισμόν' indicates direction or purpose, meaning 'in preparation for harvest' or 'ripe for harvest'.

translation: Even now the reaper receives his wages and gathers fruit for eternal life, so that the sower may rejoice together with the reaper.
notes: This sentence employs the agricultural metaphor of sowing and reaping to illustrate spiritual reward and shared joy in the work of ministry. The present participles ὁ θερίζων (the reaper) and ὁ σπείρων (the sower) function as nouns, a common feature in Koine Greek to denote the agent performing the action. The adverb ἤδη (even now) emphasizes the immediacy of the reward, contrasting with the typical expectation of delayed harvest. The purpose clause introduced by ἵνα (so that) with the present subjunctive χαιρῆ (may rejoice) indicates that the joy of the reaper is not exclusive but shared with the sower. The adverb ὁμοῦ (together) reinforces this unity of purpose and reward. The sentence structure creates a parallelism between the actions of the sower and reaper, highlighting that both participate in the same divine work and share in the same eternal outcome.

translation: For in this the word is true, that one is the sower and another the reaper.
notes: The sentence employs a clear chiasmus in its final clause: the structure 'one [A] is the sower and another [B] is the reaper' (ἄλλος ... ὁ σπείρων καὶ ἄλλος ὁ θερίζων) mirrors the semantic opposition between sowing (beginning) and reaping (conclusion). The use of the present participle (σπείρων, θερίζων) functioning as a substantive noun with the definite article highlights the enduring roles of these figures rather than a single specific action. The particle γάρ provides the causal or explanatory link to the preceding context, asserting the truth of the statement based on the logical reality of the agricultural metaphor. The phrase ὁ λόγος (the word) is used in a gnomic sense, presenting a general truth rather than a specific utterance.

translation: I have sent you to reap, yet you have not labored.
notes: This sentence employs a sharp antithesis between the active agency of the speaker ('I have sent') and the passive or inaction of the addressees ('you have not labored'). The verb 'ἀπέσταλκα' (I have sent) is in the perfect tense, indicating a completed action with continuing results—the recipients are currently in the state of having been sent. The infinitive 'θερίζειν' (to reap) functions as an object complement, specifying the purpose of the sending. The second clause contrasts this divine initiative with human failure; 'ὃ' (that which) serves as the object of the verb 'κεκοπιάκατε' (you have labored), which is also in the perfect tense, emphasizing the present state of having not engaged in the work. The negative 'οὐχ' precedes the verb for emphasis. The rhetorical structure highlights the irony that while the sender has done the work of dispatch, the recipients have not yet undertaken the work of the harvest.

translation: Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.
notes: This sentence features a striking contrast between two perfect active indicative verbs: κεκοπιακασιν (have labored/toiled) and εἰσεληλύθατε (have entered). The perfect tense here emphasizes the completed nature and enduring results of the laborers' work. The preposition εἰς with the accusative (εἰς τὸν κόπον) indicates motion into or participation in the sphere of the 'labor' or 'toil.' The construction highlights a metaphorical harvest where the addressees reap the benefits of prior spiritual or missionary work without having performed the initial struggle. Stylistically, the sentence employs asyndeton (omission of a conjunction between clauses) in some manuscript traditions, but here the coordinating conjunction καί connects the two parallel predicative clauses, creating a balanced rhythm that underscores the relationship between the sowers (others) and the reapers (you).

translation: But many from that city believed in him, the Samaritans, because of the word of the woman testifying that he had said to me all things that I did.
notes: The sentence employs the causal preposition 'dia' (διά) with the accusative case ('ton logon') to indicate the reason for the Samaritans' belief, a common construction in Koine Greek for expressing cause. The participle 'martyrousēs' (μαρτυρούσης), genitive singular feminine, agrees with 'gynaikos' (γυναικος) and functions as an attributive participle, modifying the woman and specifying the content of her testimony. This testimony is introduced by the conjunction 'hoti' (ὅτι), which introduces a direct speech clause where the woman quotes Jesus. The phrase 'panta ha epoiēsa' (πάντα ἃ ἐποίησα) is a relative clause where 'ha' (ἃ) is the neuter plural accusative object of 'epoiēsa' (ἐποίησα), referring to 'all things' (panta). The use of 'episteusan eis auton' (ἐπίστευσαν εἰς αὐτόν) is a characteristic Johannine formulation for belief, emphasizing a movement of trust into the person of Jesus rather than mere intellectual assent. The sentence begins with the postpositive particle 'de' (δέ), which connects this event to the preceding narrative, serving as a narrative transition. The syntax reflects the oral nature of the testimony being reported, with the woman's direct quote embedded within the indirect reporting of the crowd's reaction.

translation: So when the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to stay with them.
notes: The sentence begins with the temporal conjunction 'ὡς' (hōs) followed by 'οὖν' (oun), a particle often used to indicate logical consequence or to transition smoothly into the narrative action, translating here as 'so' or 'accordingly'. The verb 'ἦλθον' (ēlthon) is in the aorist indicative, marking a specific, completed action of arrival. The subject 'οἱ Σαμαρῖται' (hoi Samaritai) is a plural noun referring to the Samaritans, a group often in tension with Jewish groups in the New Testament narrative, yet here depicted as hospitable. The main verb 'ἠρώτων' (ērōton) is in the imperfect indicative, indicating a continuous or repeated action in the past (they were asking/urging), which contrasts with the punctual arrival. This imperfective aspect highlights the earnestness or persistence of their request. The verb 'μείναι' (meînai) is an aorist infinitive functioning as the object of 'ἠρώτων', a common construction where the subject of the infinitive ('αὐτόν', 'auton') is expressed separately. The prepositional phrase 'παρ' αὐτοῖς' (par' autois) uses the preposition 'παρά' (para) with the dative case to denote location 'with them' or 'in their company'. The syntax flows naturally from the temporal clause introduced by 'ὡς' to the main narrative action, demonstrating standard Koine Greek narrative structure.

translation: And he remained there two days.
notes: The verb μενέω (to remain, stay) often carries a nuance of continuing an action or state rather than a simple past event. The adverb εκεῖ (there) emphasizes the specific location established in the preceding narrative context. The temporal phrase δύο ἡμέρας is in the accusative case functioning adverbially, a common construction in Greek to denote duration of time. The sentence begins with the conjunction καί, which here serves a connective function, linking this event to the previous narrative sequence without necessarily adding emphatic force (unlike 'but' or 'even').

translation: And many more believed because of his word, and they were saying to the woman, 'It is no longer because of your conversation that we believe.'
notes: This sentence exhibits a shift in agency and source of faith. The first clause uses the aorist indicative (ἐπίστευσαν) to denote the completed act of believing triggered by 'his word' (τὸν λόγον αὐτοῦ), likely referring to Jesus' direct teaching. The second clause shifts to the imperfect indicative (ἔλεγον) for 'they were saying,' indicating a continuous or habitual action of explanation. The conjunction τε...τε (here appearing as τε following the comma and introducing the second main verb) creates a balanced connection between the two actions. The use of the demonstrative pronoun σὴν (your) in the final clause contrasts sharply with the third-person αὐτοῦ (his) in the first, highlighting the transition from the initial witness (the woman) to the direct revelation. The term λαλιά (conversation/discourse) is often used in the New Testament to denote spoken words or speech, distinguishing it from λόγος, which can imply a more substantial 'word' or 'message.' The phrase οὐκέτι (no longer) emphasizes a qualitative change in the basis of their faith, moving from reliance on a second-hand report to personal conviction.

translation: For we ourselves have heard and know that this one is truly the Savior of the world.
notes: The sentence utilizes a hendiadys-like structure where two present-perfect verbs ('have heard' and 'know') are coordinated to establish the witnesses' authority based on direct experience. The pronoun 'αὐτοί' (we ourselves) functions as an emphatic nominative, reinforcing the collective identity and certainty of the speakers. The adverb 'ἀληθῶς' (truly) modifies the copula to emphasize the genuine nature of the identification, a common rhetorical device in Johannine literature to assert theological truth. The phrase 'ὁ σωτὴρ τοῦ κόσμου' (the Savior of the world) employs the definite article twice, creating a specific, titular reference to the subject's universal role, contrasting with the more generic use of 'savior' in Hellenistic contexts.

translation: And after two days he went away from there into Galilee.
notes: The sentence begins with the temporal prepositional phrase 'μετὰ ... ἡμέρας' (after two days), a common Koine construction using the preposition 'μετά' with the accusative to denote a point in time following an event. The particle 'δέ' functions as a connective, often translated as 'and' or 'but,' serving to advance the narrative sequence from the preceding context. The verb 'ἐξῆλθεν' (he went out/away) is aorist indicative active, indicating a completed action in the past. The adverb 'ἐκεῖθεν' (from there) specifies the origin, while the prepositional phrase 'ἐς τὴν Γαλιλαίαν' (into Galilee) with the accusative case marks the destination. Stylistically, the sentence is straightforward and paratactic, typical of the Synoptic Gospel style which favors simple coordination of events over complex subordination. The geographical movement from a location previously established (often implied as Cana or a nearby region in the narrative flow) to Galilee is a standard narrative marker in the Fourth Gospel.

translation: For Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own native place.
notes: The sentence employs the emphatic pronoun αὐτός (autos) in the nominative case to highlight Jesus as the specific subject who delivered this testimony, contrasting with any potential external or third-party witnesses. The conjunction γάρ (gar) provides a causal explanation, linking this statement to a preceding context (likely the lack of recognition Jesus received in his hometown). The verb μαρτυρέω (to testify) is used in the aorist indicative, indicating a completed historical action of bearing witness. The clause introduced by ὅτι (hoti) functions as the content of the testimony, featuring a gnomic present tense verb ἔχει (he has) to express a general, timeless truth or proverb. The phrase ἐν τῇ ἰδίᾳ πατρίδι (in his own native land) utilizes the dative case of place where, modified by the intensive adjective ἴδιος (own/peculiar) to emphasize the specific and personal nature of the location. The negation οὐκ (ouk) before ἔχει creates a definitive statement of absence regarding 'timē' (honor, esteem, or price). The syntax reflects a common Semitic-influenced Greek proverbial style found in the New Testament, emphasizing the paradox of the unrecognized prophet.

translation: So when he came into Galilee, the Galileans received him, having seen all the things he had done in Jerusalem at the festival.
notes: The sentence employs a temporal clause introduced by ὡς οὖν ('so when'), a common narrative formula in the Fourth Gospel to mark a transition in the story. The main clause features a periphrastic reception: the Galileans 'received' (ἔδεξαντο) Jesus, a term often implying hospitality or acceptance. This reception is explained by a preceding aorist active participle, ὁράκοτες ('having seen'), which functions as a causal adjunct, indicating that their welcome was based on their prior observation of his miracles. The participle governs a neuter plural object (πάντα), which is further modified by a relative clause (ἃ ἐποίησεν). The relative pronoun ἃ ('which') is placed in the object position of the relative clause verb ἐποίησεν ('he did'), a standard syntactic structure. The prepositional phrases ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις and ἐν τῇ ἑορτῇ ('in Jerusalem' and 'at the festival') are stacked to specify the location and timing of the prior events. The repetition of the preposition ἐν for distinct locative/dative complements adds clarity and rhythm to the sentence. The use of the imperfect or aorist tense in the relative clause versus the aorist in the main narrative creates a clear temporal sequence: first the deeds in Jerusalem, then the arrival in Galilee, and finally the reception.

translation: For they also came to the festival.
notes: The sentence features the postpositive particle γάρ (for), which typically appears in the second position of its clause, here following the connective καί (also/and) and the subject αὐτοί. The use of the enclitic καί (as opposed to the non-enclitic conjunction) alongside αὐτοί creates a specific emphatic nuance, often translated as 'even they' or simply 'they also,' indicating that the subject performed this action in addition to others or despite circumstances. The verb ἦλθον (aorist indicative of ἔρχομαι) denotes a simple, completed action of arrival. The preposition εἰς with the accusative noun τὴν ἑορτήν marks the direction of motion toward the festival. Stylistically, the sentence is concise and direct, characteristic of the narrative style found in the New Testament, focusing on the factual movement of the subjects into a specific religious context.

translation: So he came again to Cana of Galilee, where he had made the water into wine.
notes: The particle οὖν functions here as a connective adverb, linking this event to a preceding narrative sequence (likely the calling of Philip and Nathanael) by indicating logical consequence or narrative progression ('therefore' or 'so'). The adverb πάλιν ('again') highlights the return to a previously visited location, creating a narrative frame. The phrase ἔνθα ('where') introduces a relative clause of place that serves as a narrative flashback or parenthetical reference to the miracle of Cana (John 2:1-11). The verb ποιεῖν with the accusative and accusative complement (οἶνον) denotes a transformation or making of one thing into another. Stylistically, the sentence employs an anaphoric reference to the miracle, grounding the current narrative in the reader's prior knowledge of the text. The use of the aorist indicative (ἤλθεν, ἐποίησεν) marks these as completed historical actions within the gospel narrative.

translation: A royal official had a son who was ill in Capernaum.
notes: The sentence utilizes a relative clause (οὑ ὁ υἱὸς ἠσθένει) to provide essential descriptive information about the 'son' without a relative pronoun introducing a new subject, a common feature in Koine Greek narrative where the relative pronoun ὁς (here ὁ) functions as a connective. The verb ἠσθένει (he was ill) is in the imperfect indicative, indicating a continuous or ongoing state of sickness, which sets the dramatic tension for the subsequent healing narrative. The term βασιλικός (royal official/official of the king) is a specific title often used in the Septuagint and New Testament to denote a courtier or servant of a king (in this context, likely Herod Antipas), distinguishing this character from a generic 'man.' The syntax places the location (ἐν Καφαρναούμ) at the end of the sentence, a typical Greek rhetorical device called 'end-weight,' emphasizing the setting where the miracle will unfold. There is no chiasmus or asyndeton here; the flow is straightforward and narrative, characteristic of the Johannine style which often introduces characters and their crises with concise, direct syntax.

translation: This man, having heard that Jesus was coming from Judea into Galilee, went to him and asked him to come down and heal his son.
notes: The sentence features an aorist participle (ἀκούσας) functioning adverbially to indicate the cause or circumstance of the main action, a common structure in Koine Greek narrative. The main verbs (ἀπῆλθεν and ἠρώτα) are connected by a simple conjunction (καί), creating a rhythmic sequence of actions. The request made by the man is expressed through a purpose clause introduced by ἵνα with two subjunctive verbs (καταβῇ and ἰάσηται) coordinated by καί; this double subjunctive emphasizes the interconnected nature of the request (the descent is the means to the healing). The use of the demonstrative pronoun οὗτος (this man) at the very beginning of the sentence serves to draw specific attention to the individual's identity or presence in the immediate context, often implying a sense of immediacy or importance. The prepositional phrases (ἐκ... εἰς...) clearly delineate the geographical movement of Jesus, highlighting the transition from the southern region of Judea to the northern region of Galilee, a significant detail for the narrative's geography.

translation: For he was about to die.
notes: The verb μέλλω (mellō) with the infinitive ἀποθνῄσκειν (apothnēskein) forms a periphrastic construction indicating imminent future action, literally 'he was about to die' or 'he was on the point of dying.' The particle γάρ (gar) provides a causal or explanatory link to the preceding context, meaning 'for' or 'because.' The syntax reflects a common Hellenistic Greek pattern where the future meaning is derived from the combination of the imperfect of μέλλω and the present infinitive. The use of the imperfect tense here emphasizes the ongoing nature of the impending event at the time of narration. This construction is frequent in the New Testament to describe events on the verge of happening, often carrying a tone of inevitability or divine foreknowledge.

translation: Jesus therefore said to him.
notes: The particle οὖν (oun) is an inferential or connective particle that often indicates a logical conclusion or a transition in the narrative flow, here linking Jesus' statement to the preceding context. The verb εἶπεν (eipen) is the aorist indicative active of λέγω (legō), meaning 'to say' or 'to speak.' In the Fourth Gospel, the aorist tense is frequently used for simple narrative statements of speech acts. The preposition πρός (pros) with the accusative case (αὐτόν) indicates direction or the recipient of the action, translated here as 'to him.' The definite article ὁ (ho) preceding Ἰησοῦς (Iēsous) serves to identify the specific subject, Jesus, while αὐτόν (auton) functions as a third-person singular masculine accusative pronoun, referring to the interlocutor previously mentioned in the dialogue (Nicodemus in this specific biblical context). The sentence structure is straightforward, employing a standard Subject-Verb-Prepositional Phrase order common in Koine Greek narrative.

translation: Unless you see signs and wonders, you will by no means believe.
notes: This sentence employs a strong first-class conditional structure (εἰ + subjunctive, here introduced by ἄν) to express a necessary condition for belief. The verb ἴδητε is aorist subjunctive, indicating a specific, completed action upon which the main clause depends. The main clause utilizes the emphatic negative construction οὐ μή + subjunctive (πιστεύσητε), which is a hallmark of Koine Greek (particularly in the New Testament) to express an absolute, future negation—here translating to 'you will by no means believe' or 'you will never believe.' The phrase 'signs and wonders' (σημεῖα καὶ τέρατα) is a hendiadys often used in biblical and Septuagintal contexts to describe divine manifestations; 'signs' (σημεῖα) typically refer to meaningful indicators of a higher power, while 'wonders' (τέρατα) emphasize the miraculous or terrifying nature of the event. The sentence lacks a stated subject for the verbs, which are both second person plural, implying a collective audience. The syntactic parallelism between the conditional clause and the main clause creates a stark logical contrast: the absence of miraculous evidence results in absolute unbelief.

translation: The official said to him.
notes: The verb 'λέγει' (he says) is in the present indicative active, a tense often used in the Fourth Gospel (John) to create a vivid, dramatic immediacy, drawing the reader into the conversation as it unfolds. The subject 'ὁ βασιλικός' (the official) is an adjective substantivized by the definite article 'ὁ', a common construction in Koine Greek referring to a royal official or courtier. The preposition 'πρός' (towards/with) governs the accusative pronoun 'αὐτόν' (him), indicating the direction of the speech. The syntax places the subject at the end of the clause (verb-object-subject order), a stylistic choice that emphasizes the action of speaking and the identity of the speaker in a narrative context.

translation: Sir, come down before my child dies.
notes: The vocative 'κύριε' (Sir/Lord) is used here as a direct address to Jesus, reflecting the social deference of the petitioner (a royal official) rather than necessarily a full theological title of divinity at this specific moment of desperation. The verb 'κατάβηθι' is an aorist imperative, conveying an urgent command for immediate action. The conjunction 'πρίν' (before) introduces a temporal clause with the future infinitive 'ἀποθανεῖν' (to die). In Koine Greek, 'πρίν' is frequently followed by the infinitive to denote an action that has not yet occurred but is anticipated, functioning similarly to 'before' + future indicative in English. The phrase 'τὸ παιδίον μου' (my child) emphasizes the personal stake of the father. The syntax is concise and direct, characteristic of the narrative style in the Gospel of John, where dialogue often drives the plot through urgent petitions and divine responses.

translation: Jesus said to him.
notes: The verb λέγει (3rd person singular present indicative active) denotes a present action within a narrative context, a usage known as the 'narrative present' or 'historic present,' which serves to vividly bring the dialogue into the immediate moment. The construction features the verb with a dative object (αὐτῷ) indicating the recipient of the speech. The subject (ὁ Ἰησοῦς) follows the verb, a common word order in Koine Greek that places emphasis on the agent performing the action. The definite article (ὁ) is used with the proper name Ἰησοῦς, which is standard in this period to denote a specific, well-known individual.

translation: Go!
notes: The verb πορεύου is a second person singular present middle imperative of πορεύω. In the middle voice with this imperative form, it carries the sense of 'go yourself' or 'proceed,' functioning as a direct command. The present tense indicates an immediate or continuous action. The sentence relies entirely on the imperative mood to convey urgency or authority, a common feature in narrative commands where the subject (you) is implicit. There are no conjunctions or additional clauses, creating a stark, asyndetic command typical of direct speech in biblical and Hellenistic texts.

translation: Your son is alive.
notes: This sentence employs the present indicative active of ζάω (to live), which here functions as a stative verb meaning 'to be alive' or 'to be living,' contrasting with a state of death. The construction is a simple subject-predicate sentence where the definite article ὁ agrees with the masculine singular noun υἱός (son), modified by the possessive pronoun σου (your). The syntax is straightforward, with no subordinate clauses or complex embeddings. The phrase likely appears in a context of relief or restoration, such as a report of recovery from illness or death, common in Johannine miracle narratives. The brevity of the statement, using only four words, creates an emphatic and immediate declaration of life.

translation: The man believed the word that Jesus had spoken to him, and he went his way.
notes: This sentence features two main clauses coordinated by the conjunction 'kai' (and). The first clause uses the aorist indicative active 'episteusen' (he believed), indicating a punctual, completed action of faith. The object of this belief is 'ton logon' (the word), modified by a relative clause 'hon eipen' (which he spoke). Notably, the relative pronoun 'hon' is in the accusative case, functioning as the direct object of the verb 'eipen' (he spoke), while the subject of 'eipen' is 'Iesous' (Jesus). The second clause uses the imperfect indicative middle 'eporeueto' (he was going/went his way), which often implies a continuous or habitual action, here suggesting the man's departure or continued journey after his conversion. The use of the imperfect alongside the aorist in the first clause creates a narrative flow where the decisive act of belief is followed by the ongoing state of the man's life. The phrase 'he went his way' is a common biblical idiom indicating the man's departure or the beginning of a new path in life, often used to signify the completion of a transformative encounter.

translation: Now, while he was going down, his slaves met him and reported that his son was living.
notes: The sentence features a temporal clause introduced by the genitive absolute construction (καταβαίνοντος... αὐτοῦ), which sets the scene for the main actions. The particle δέ serves as a connective, often translating as 'now' or 'but,' linking this event to the preceding narrative context. The verb ὑπαντάω (to meet) is frequently used in contexts of honorific greeting or urgent arrival. The conjunction καί links two coordinated main verbs (ὑπήντησαν and ἤγγειλαν) without a pause, creating a rapid narrative flow. The subordinate clause introduced by ὅτι (that) reports the content of the message. The verb ζῇ (he is living) is in the present indicative, which in this context emphasizes the current, ongoing reality of the child's life as opposed to a past state, confirming the immediate success of the healing. The use of δοῦλοι (slaves/servants) highlights the social hierarchy and the role of intermediaries in conveying news to a person of status.

translation: He inquired, therefore, about the hour, which they had kept in a more polished manner.
notes: The verb πυνθάνομαι (to inquire, ask) is used in the middle voice (ἐπυθέτο), a common construction for seeking information. The particle οὖν (therefore, then) serves as a connective, linking this action to the preceding narrative context. The phrase παρ' αὐτῶν (from them/by them) indicates the source of the information regarding the hour. The relative clause (ἣν... ἔσχεν) modifies 'hour' (ὥραν), though the relative pronoun ἣν is elided in the provided text, implied by the preposition ἐν and the adjective κομψότερον functioning as a predicate adjective. The adjective κομψότερον (more polished/refined) is a comparative form describing the manner in which the hour was kept or observed. In a cultural context, the 'polished' or 'refined' manner of keeping time may allude to the precision or social propriety associated with the timing of a meal or a gathering, reflecting the social customs of the time where punctuality or the specific timing of events held significance. The sentence structure is straightforward, with the main clause followed by a participial or relative construction that provides additional detail about the subject's observation.

translation: So they said to him, 'Yesterday at the seventh hour he was left by the fever.'
notes: The sentence features the discourse particle οὖν (oun), which serves a connective function, linking this statement to the preceding narrative context. The verb ἔλεγον (here in the aorist indicative active εἶπον, though the lemma is λέγω) introduces direct speech. The adverbial phrase ἔχθες ὥραν ἑβδόμην (yesterday the seventh hour) is a specific temporal construction common in Koine Greek for denoting precise times of day, counting hours from sunrise. The syntax employs a passive construction (ἀφῆκεν... ὁ πυρετός, literally 'the fever left him'), which is a standard idiom in Greek for the cessation of an illness, where the disease is the grammatical subject performing the action of departing. The word order places the temporal modifier before the verb, emphasizing the specific moment of the miracle.

translation: So the Father knew that in that hour Jesus had spoken to him.
notes: The sentence employs the temporal phrase 'in that hour' (ἐν ᾗ ὥρᾳ), where the relative pronoun ᾗ agrees in case, number, and gender with ὥρα, functioning adverbially to specify the precise moment of the action. The verb ἐγνώσκει (here aorist ἐγνώ) denotes a sudden or definitive realization or recognition, often implying a deepening of understanding. The subordinate clause introduced by ὅτι reports the content of this knowledge, with the aorist εἶπεν indicating a completed action that occurred at that specific time. The construction emphasizes the Father's awareness of the exact moment Jesus spoke, highlighting the theological theme of divine omniscience and the precise timing of Jesus' revelation. The use of οὖν (so/therefore) at the beginning links this realization to the preceding narrative, suggesting a logical consequence or conclusion drawn from prior events.

translation: Your son lives.
notes: This sentence utilizes the verb 'ζάω' (to live) in the third person singular present indicative active, a form that can denote both physical vitality and continued existence. The construction is a simple subject-predicate sentence where 'ὁ υἱός' (the son) is the subject and 'σου' (your) functions as a possessive attribute modifying the subject. The use of the definite article 'ὁ' emphasizes the specific individual being referred to. The sentence is grammatically complete, relying on context to establish the identity of the 'son' and the addressee 'you'. No literary devices such as chiasmus or asyndeton are present in this brief utterance; it is a direct declarative statement.

translation: And he believed, and his whole household believed.
notes: This sentence exhibits a classic case of asyndeton (omission of a conjunction) in the second clause if one were to expect a verb, but here the conjunction 'kai' (and) is explicitly repeated, creating a parallel structure (anaphora of the conjunction). The verb 'episteusen' (he believed) is elliptical in the second clause; the subject 'his whole household' is new, but the verb is understood from the first clause. The phrase 'his whole household' (hē oikia autou holē) uses the adjective 'holē' (whole/all) in the nominative feminine singular to agree with 'oikia'. In the cultural and religious context of the New Testament, the belief of the 'whole household' signifies a collective conversion, often implying that the head of the household's faith extended to the entire domestic unit, a common motif in early Christian conversion narratives. The word order places the adjective 'holē' at the end for emphasis, highlighting the totality of the household's conversion.

translation: This was the second sign that Jesus performed, having come from Judea into Galilee.
notes: The sentence employs a periphrastic temporal structure using the aorist active participle 'ἐλθών' (having come), which modifies the main verb 'ἐποίησεν' (performed) to establish the sequence of events. The demonstrative 'τοῦτο' (this) at the beginning of the sentence creates a strong anaphoric link to a preceding sign, emphasizing continuity within a narrative sequence. The adjective 'δεύτερον' (second) functions attributively with 'σημεῖον' (sign), a term in Johannine literature that specifically denotes a miraculous work revealing divine glory, rather than a mere omen. The geographical progression from 'Ἰουδαίας' (Judea) to 'Γαλιλαίας' (Galilee) marks a significant narrative shift, often associated in this Gospel with the transition from the initial public ministry in the south to the more extensive mission in the north. The word order places the object 'τοῦτο' and the modifier 'δεύτερον' at the front for emphasis, highlighting the significance of the miracle's ordinal position in the author's theological structure.

translation: After these things, there was a festival of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.
notes: The phrase 'μετὰ ταῦτα' (after these things) is a standard formulaic transition in the Gospel of John used to advance the narrative sequence between pericopes, functioning similarly to 'afterward' or 'subsequently.' The verb 'ἦν' (there was) is in the imperfect tense, indicating a state of being or ongoing duration, which sets the temporal scene for the subsequent action. The preposition 'εἰς' (into/up to) with the accusative 'Ἰερουσαλήμ' denotes motion toward a destination. In the context of Judean geography and culture, the verb 'ἀνέβη' (he went up) is idiomatic; Jerusalem is situated at a higher elevation than Galilee and the surrounding regions, so 'going up' is the standard directional marker for travel to the holy city, reflecting both physical topography and spiritual significance. The sentence utilizes a simple paratactic structure connected by 'καί' (and), linking the setting (the festival) directly to the protagonist's movement without subordination.

translation: Now there is in Jerusalem a pool called in Hebrew Bethzatha, which has five porticoes.
notes: The sentence utilizes a present indicative verb (ἔστιν) to describe a current state or existence, a common feature in descriptive passages. The adverbial particle δέ serves as a connective, often translated as 'now' or 'but' to signal a continuation or slight shift in the narrative flow. The phrase ἐν τοῖς Ἱεροσολύμοις demonstrates the use of the dative plural for the city name, a standard Attic and Koine convention for 'in Jerusalem'. The term προβατικῇ (to the sheep) is a distinctive epithet for the pool, likely referring to its association with the slaughter of sacrificial animals or the washing of animals before sacrifice, reflecting the ritual purity practices of Second Temple Judaism. The construction τοῦ λεγομένου (called) with the genitive of the language (Ἑβραϊστὶ) followed by the proper name is a standard idiom for providing etymological or vernacular equivalents. The participle ἔχουσα (having) functions adjectivally to modify the pool, providing architectural detail. The specific mention of 'five porticoes' (πέντε στοάς) is a precise geographical and architectural marker used by the author to authenticate the setting for readers familiar with Jerusalem's topography.

translation: In these [places] lay a multitude of the sick, of the blind, of the lame, of the withered.
notes: The sentence employs a cumulative list of genitive adjectives (τυφλῶν, χωλῶν, ξηρῶν) modifying the genitive plural participle ἁσθενούντων ('of the sick'), creating a rhythmic enumeration of physical ailments. The use of the aorist imperfect κατέκειτο ('was lying') emphasizes the continuous state of the crowd. The adjective ξηρῶν ('withered') is particularly significant in this medical and cultural context, likely referring to those suffering from dryness or wasting diseases, distinct from the paralysis implied by χωλῶν ('lame'). The sentence utilizes asyndeton (the omission of conjunctions) in the list of ailments, which accelerates the pace and creates a stark, cumulative effect, highlighting the sheer variety and density of suffering present.

translation: And there was a certain man there, having thirty-eight years in his infirmity.
notes: The sentence employs a paratactic structure common in Koine Greek narrative, initiated by the connective particle 'δέ' (de), which serves to continue the narrative thread. The indefinite pronoun 'τις' (tis) combined with 'ἄνθρωπος' (anthrōpos) functions as a specific indefinite, introducing a character who is not yet named, a technique often used to build suspense or focus attention on the individual's condition rather than their identity. The verb 'ἦν' (ēn) sets the temporal and existential scene. The participle 'ἔχων' (echōn), meaning 'having', is a present active participle that functions adjectivally to modify 'ἄνθρωπος', providing a descriptive detail about the subject's state. The phrase 'in his infirmity' uses the preposition 'ἐν' (en) with the dative case ('ἀσθενείᾳ') to denote the sphere or condition in which the man existed. The possessive pronoun 'αὐτοῦ' (autou) agrees with 'ἀσθενείᾳ' and emphasizes the personal nature of his suffering. The specific age of thirty-eight years is historically and medically significant in ancient literature, often associated with a long period of suffering, contrasting with the traditional lifespan of seventy or eighty years mentioned in Psalms, thereby highlighting the man's endurance. The syntax places the duration of the suffering ('thirty-eight years') immediately before the state ('in his infirmity'), creating a direct link between the length of time and the nature of the affliction.

translation: Seeing this one lying down, and having realized that he had already been there for a long time, Jesus said to him.
notes: The sentence employs two aorist participles (ἰδών, γνούς) functioning adverbially to describe the sequence of Jesus' actions prior to the main verb λέγει. The participle ἰδών takes the accusative object τοῦτον and the accusative present participle κατακείμενον as its object, a construction indicating the state of the object perceived. The phrase ἔχει χρόνον (literally 'he has time') is an idiomatic expression for duration of stay. The adverb ἤδη emphasizes that a significant period has already elapsed. The syntactic structure creates a concise narrative flow where observation and cognitive realization precede the spoken response, a common feature in Koine Greek narrative to establish immediacy.

translation: Do you wish to become well?
notes: The sentence utilizes a future infinitive (γενέσθαι) functioning as the object of the verb 'to wish' (θέλεις), a construction common in Greek to express desire for a future state or action. The predicate adjective υγιής (healthy, well) is in the nominative case, agreeing with the implied subject of the infinitive (the person addressed). The use of the interrogative particle is absent, relying instead on the intonation indicated by the question mark to form a direct question. This structure reflects a direct, personal inquiry regarding the recipient's desire for physical restoration, typical of healing narratives in ancient literature where the patient's agency or consent is often highlighted.

translation: The one who was weak answered him.
notes: The sentence features a participle in the imperfect active, 'ἀσθενῶν' (from ἀσθενέω), functioning as a substantive noun modified by the definite article 'ὁ'. This construction ('ὁ + participle') is a common syntactic strategy in Ancient Greek to nominalize a verbal idea, effectively creating the meaning 'the weak one' or 'the one who was weak.' The verb 'ἀπεκρίθη' is an aorist middle indicative, which in this context carries a passive sense ('was answered' or simply 'answered'), a standard usage for the verb ἀποκρίνομαι when followed by a direct object (here, the dative 'αὐτῷ') or when the subject is the recipient of a prior question. The dative 'αὐτῷ' indicates the person to whom the response was directed. The sentence structure is simple and direct, typical of narrative prose, emphasizing the identity of the responder through their state of weakness.

translation: Sir, I have no man, so that whenever the water is stirred up, he may throw me into the pool.
notes: The sentence employs a direct address (κύριε) in the vocative case, indicating the speaker is speaking to a figure of authority or respect. The main clause uses the verb ἔχω (I have) with a negative particle οὐκ and an accusative object ἄνθρωπον (a man/person), establishing a state of lacking human assistance. The syntax then shifts to a purpose clause introduced by ἵνα (so that/in order that), which is governed by the main verb. Within this purpose clause, a temporal conditional structure is created by ὅταν (whenever) followed by the aorist passive subjunctive ταραχθῇ (may be stirred up), referring to the disturbance of the water. The main verb of this subordinate clause is βάλη (may throw), also in the aorist active subjunctive, taking the speaker (με) as its object and the pool (κολυμβηθραν) as the destination via the preposition εἰς. The term κολυμβηθραν refers to a pool or bathing place, specifically alluding to the Pool of Bethesda in the Gospel of John, where healing was believed to occur when the water was stirred. The sentence structure highlights a dramatic irony or a plea for intervention, where the speaker's lack of human aid prevents them from reaching the healing waters in time.

translation: In whom, however, I come, another descends before me.
notes: The sentence employs a relative clause introduced by 'ἐν ᾧ' (in whom), referring to a specific individual previously mentioned in the broader context. The particle 'δέ' functions as a connective, often translating as 'however' or 'but,' indicating a contrast or continuation of thought. The structure juxtaposes the speaker's arrival ('I come') with the descent of 'another' who is 'before' the speaker, highlighting a hierarchy or precedence. This construction may reflect a theological or hierarchical distinction, emphasizing the relative status of the two figures involved. The use of the present tense for 'I come' and the aorist indicative for 'descends' suggests a narrative or declarative tone, underscoring the immediacy of the action.

translation: Jesus said to him.
notes: The sentence exhibits a standard Greek word order where the verb (λέγει) precedes its subject (ὁ Ἰησοῦς), a common feature in narrative contexts that places emphasis on the action of speaking. The dative pronoun αὐτῷ functions as an indirect object, indicating the recipient of the speech. The use of the definite article ὁ before the proper noun Ἰησοῦς is typical in Koine Greek to identify a specific, known individual, functioning similarly to a title or definite reference within the narrative flow. The verb is in the present indicative active, which in Greek narrative often denotes the 'historical present,' a stylistic device used to make past events feel immediate and vivid to the reader.

translation: Rise, take up your mat and walk.
notes: This sentence consists of a series of three aorist imperatives (ἔγειρε, ἆρον, περιπάτει) linked by the conjunction καί, creating a rapid, forceful rhythm characteristic of divine commands in the New Testament. The noun κράβαττος (krabattos) is a specific term for a small portable bed or mat, distinct from the larger κλίνη (klinē), often associated with the sick or the poor. The command to 'take up' the object one is lying upon implies an immediate transition from a state of passivity or infirmity to active movement, symbolizing a complete restoration of health and autonomy. The syntax is paratactic, relying on the conjunction 'and' to chain the actions together without subordination, emphasizing the sequential and inevitable nature of the miracle.

translation: And the man became healthy, and he picked up his mat and walked around.
notes: The sentence employs a tripartite structure connected by the repetitive conjunction 'kai' (and), a stylistic feature often found in Koine Greek narrative known as parataxis. The verb 'egeneto' (became) is a deponent imperfect, indicating a process of change into the state described by the predicate adjective 'hygiēs' (healthy/whole). The noun 'krabatton' (mat) is a specific term for a portable bed or mat, carrying cultural significance as a symbol of the man's previous infirmity and dependence. The final verb 'peripatei' (walked around) is in the imperfect tense, which here describes a continuous or habitual action resulting from the healing, emphasizing the restoration of mobility. The sequence of actions—becoming whole, lifting the bed, and walking—demonstrates a logical progression from physical cure to the demonstration of that cure.

translation: It was a Sabbath on that day.
notes: The sentence utilizes the imperfect indicative of εἰμί (ἦν) to establish a background state or setting, a common feature in Hellenistic Greek narrative. The particle δέ follows the verb (enclitic position) to provide a connective function, often translating as 'now' or 'but,' marking a transition or specifying the temporal context of the narrative. The phrase ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ functions as an adverbial modifier of time. The use of the article ἡ in ἡ ἡμέρα is anaphoric, referring back to a previously mentioned day or a specific day within the immediate narrative context. The construction places emphasis on the specific day being a Sabbath, which is theologically significant in the Johannine context, often used to frame legal or religious conflicts.

translation: So the Jews said to the one who had been healed.
notes: The sentence begins with the inferential particle οὖν (oun), indicating that this statement is a logical consequence or a continuation of the preceding narrative context. The verb ἐλέγον (elegen) is in the imperfect tense, suggesting either an ongoing action or a repeated action in the past (iterative), often translated as 'were saying' or 'kept saying,' which fits the context of a dialogue or interrogation. The subject οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι (hoi Ioudaioi) refers to the Jewish religious authorities or opponents in the narrative. The object is not a direct person but a participle, τῷ τεθεραπευμένῳ (tōi therapeuménō), a dative singular masculine perfect passive participle of θεραπεύω (therapeuō, 'to heal' or 'to serve'). The use of the perfect tense here emphasizes the completed state of the healing: the man is 'the one who has been healed' or 'the one who is now healed.' The construction uses the dative case for the indirect object (the recipient of the speech), which is standard for verbs of speaking in Ancient Greek. The phrase relies on the article τῷ to nominalize the participle, functioning as 'the one who...'. There are no overt literary devices like chiasmus or asyndeton in this specific clause, but the syntax highlights the contrast between the active agents (the Jews speaking) and the passive recipient of the miracle (the healed man).

translation: It is a Sabbath, and it is not lawful for you to lift up your pallet.
notes: This sentence features a paratactic structure joined by the coordinating conjunction 'kai' (and), creating a direct juxtaposition of the temporal setting and the legal prohibition. The verb 'estin' (is) functions as a predicate nominative to 'sabbaton' (Sabbath), establishing the time of the discourse. The core of the sentence relies on the impersonal verb 'exestin' (it is lawful/permitted), which governs a dative of the person ('soi', for you) and an infinitive in the subject position ('airein', to lift up). The use of the infinitive 'airein' as the subject of 'exestin' is a classic construction in Koine Greek for expressing permission or ability. The term 'krabbattos' (pallet/bed) refers to a portable mat or bed, often associated with the sick or those in a state of repose, and its mention here is culturally significant in the context of healing and the Sabbath laws regarding carrying burdens. The negative 'ouk' precedes the verb to negate the possibility of the action. The sentence employs a clear contrast between the sanctity of the day and the restriction placed on the individual's physical action.

translation: He answered them.
notes: The verb ἀπεκρίθη is the aorist middle indicative third person singular of ἀποκρίνω. In the context of the New Testament, this aorist form often denotes a specific, decisive response to a preceding inquiry or situation. The middle voice (or sometimes deponent usage in this specific verb) can imply a response that is reflexive in nature—answering *for oneself* or *on one's own authority*—or simply functions as a standard deponent form in Koine Greek where the middle morphology is retained despite lacking distinct middle semantics. The pronoun αὐτοῖς is dative plural, functioning as the indirect object of the verb, indicating the recipients of the speech. The sentence is syntactically simple, consisting of a finite verb and its object, lacking a subject pronoun because the third person singular ending of the verb suffices to identify the subject (he/she/it), a common feature in Greek known as pro-drop.

translation: The one who made me well, he said to me.
notes: This sentence features a participle construction (ποιησας, aorist active participle) functioning as a substantive noun phrase, modified by the definite article (ο), which is a common feature in Koine Greek to nominalize actions. The verb εἶπεν (said) is in the aorist indicative, indicating a specific past action. The pronoun ἐκεῖνος (that one/he) serves as a resumptive subject for the main verb, emphasizing the agent of the speaking action, a stylistic choice often found in narrative texts to clarify or highlight the subject after a long modifier. The construction highlights the causality between the healing and the instruction received, a recurring theme in Johannine literature where the identity of the healer is intrinsically linked to the authority of their words.

translation: Pick up your mat and walk.
notes: This sentence consists of two imperative verbs (ἆρον, 'pick up/lift'; περιπάτει, 'walk') coordinated by the conjunction καί ('and'), forming a compound command. The verb ἀείρω (here in the aorist imperative) literally means 'to lift' or 'to take up,' while κράβαττος refers specifically to a portable bed or mat, a common item in antiquity for resting. The use of the singular possessive pronoun σου ('your') emphasizes personal responsibility. The command to 'walk' immediately after lifting the bed is a notable syntactic and semantic feature, as it implies an immediate transition from a state of rest or incapacity to one of active movement, a rhetorical device often used to underscore the power of the command or the immediacy of the healing. The brevity and directness of the sentence, lacking any intervening clauses or descriptive phrases, create a sense of urgency and authority.

translation: They asked him.
notes: The verb ἠρώτησαν (aorist active indicative, 3rd person plural) denotes a specific, completed act of questioning, common in narrative contexts. The pronoun αὐτόν (accusative masculine singular) serves as the direct object, referring to a male individual previously mentioned or implied in the discourse. The sentence is an independent clause functioning as a complete narrative unit, typical of the concise, paratactic style found in the Johannine narrative, where questions and answers drive the dialogue forward without extensive elaboration.

translation: Who is the man who says to you?
notes: The sentence features a relative clause (ὁ εἰπών σοι) modifying the subject 'man' (ἄνθρωπος). The participle 'saying' (εἰπών) is in the present active form, indicating ongoing or habitual action. The use of 'to you' (σοι) in the dative case highlights a direct address, which is common in dialogic contexts. The sentence structure is straightforward, with the relative pronoun 'who' (ὁ) connecting the main clause to the descriptive clause. The tone is interrogative, suggesting a question about the identity or authority of the person speaking.

translation: Lift [it] and walk!
notes: This sentence consists of two aorist active imperatives, αἴρε (ἆρον) and περιπάτει, coordinated by the particle καί. The first verb, αἴρε, is the standard aorist imperative of αἴρω ('to lift'), while περιπάτει is the present imperative of περιπατέω ('to walk'). The omission of the direct object (typically 'your mat' or 'bed') in the first clause is a common feature of imperative constructions where the object is understood from the immediate context (ellipsis). The use of the present imperative for 'walk' alongside the aorist for 'lift' creates a subtle aspectual contrast: the lifting is a punctual, completed action required to enable the continuous action of walking. The sentence exhibits asyndeton in spirit (though explicitly connected by καί here) by presenting a sequence of commands without explanatory clauses, creating a tone of urgent authority.

translation: But the one who was sick did not know who he was.
notes: The sentence features the connective particle δέ (de) attached to the article ὁ (ho), creating the enclitic form ὁ δέ, which functions here as a transitional phrase ('but the one...') to shift focus from the previous context to this specific individual. The verb ἠδεῖ (ēde) is the imperfect indicative of οἶδα (to know), used in the sense of 'did not know' or 'was unaware.' In Classical and Koine Greek, οἶδα often takes a direct object clause (ὅτι) or, as seen here, an indirect question introduced by τίς (who) with the infinitive or finite verb εἶναι (to be). The construction τίς ἐστιν (who he is) functions as the object of knowing. The phrase ὁ ἀσθενῶν uses the present active participle of ἀσθενέω (to be sick/weak) with the article, effectively nominalizing the adjective to mean 'the sick one' or 'the one who was sick.' The syntax reflects a common narrative structure in the Gospel of John where physical healing is juxtaposed with spiritual ignorance or lack of recognition.

translation: For Jesus had withdrawn, a crowd being in that place.
notes: The sentence employs an absolute genitive construction (ὄχλου ὄντος), where the genitive noun (ὄχλου) and its accompanying participle (ὄντος) stand independently of the main clause's syntax, providing background information regarding the circumstances under which the main action occurred. The verb ἐκνεύω (to withdraw or move away) is a compound of ἐκ (out of) and νεύω (to nod or move), often used to describe a tactical retreat or a deliberate separation from a location. The use of the causal conjunction γάρ (for) indicates that this statement provides an explanation or justification for a preceding action or situation. The phrase ἐν τῷ τόπῳ (in that place) uses the definite article τῷ with the noun τόπος to specify a particular, previously mentioned or contextually understood location. The sentence structure reflects a common narrative technique in Hellenistic Greek, particularly in the New Testament, where absolute constructions are used to maintain narrative flow while introducing contextual details without breaking the main clause's momentum.

translation: After these things, Jesus found him in the temple and said to him.
notes: The phrase 'μετα ταῦτα' (after these things) is a standard narrative formula in Koine Greek, particularly in the Gospel of John, used to mark a transition to a new episode or to signal that an action follows a previously mentioned event. The verb 'εὑρίσκει' (finds) is in the present tense (historical present), a stylistic device common in ancient historiography and narrative that vividly brings past events into the immediate experience of the reader. The prepositional phrase 'ἐν τῷ ἱερῷ' (in the temple) utilizes the definite article 'τῷ' with the adjective 'ἱερῷ' functioning as a substantive noun, referring to the entire sacred precinct rather than a specific building. The sentence employs asyndeton (the omission of conjunctions between clauses) in the second half of the narrative flow, though here the conjunction 'καὶ' is present to coordinate the two main actions ('found' and 'said'), creating a balanced, sequential rhythm typical of Johannine dialogue introductions. The use of the aorist 'εἶπεν' (said) for the second verb marks a completed action following the ongoing state implied by the historical present 'εὑρίσκει'.

translation: Behold, you have become whole.
notes: The sentence begins with 'ἴδε' (behold/look), a second-person singular aorist imperative of ὁράω used here as an exclamation to draw attention to the miracle or state being described. The adjective 'ὑγιής' (healthy, whole, sound) functions as a predicative nominative complement to the verb 'γεγόνας' (you have become), which is the second-person singular perfect active indicative of γίνομαι. The use of the perfect tense emphasizes the resulting state of wholeness rather than the action of becoming. This construction highlights a completed transformation from a previous state of infirmity to one of health, a common theme in healing narratives within the New Testament.

translation: Sin no more, so that something worse does not happen to you.
notes: This sentence features a present imperative (ἁμάρτανε) functioning as a command to cease an ongoing action, paired with a final clause introduced by ἵνα ('so that'). The subjunctive verb γένηται ('may happen' or 'happen') in the ἵνα-clause expresses purpose or result. The adjective χεῖρόν (worse) is the neuter comparative of κακός, serving as the subject of the final clause, while τι (something) acts as an indefinite attributive modifying it. The dative pronoun σοι (to you) indicates the recipient of the potential harm. Stylistically, the construction employs a concise warning common in Johannine literature, using the indefinite τι to create a sense of unspecified but imminent danger.

translation: The man went away and said to the Jews that Jesus is the one who made him well.
notes: The sentence employs a simple coordinate structure joined by 'and' (καί) linking two aorist indicative verbs (ἀπῆλθεν, εἶπεν), creating a rapid narrative progression typical of Johannine style. The phrase 'made him well' uses the aorist participle ποιήσας with the accusative object αὐτόν and a predicate adjective (ὑγιῆ), a construction where the participle functions substantively to identify the agent. The use of 'the Jews' (τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις) in the dative case as the indirect object of 'said' reflects the specific Johannine tendency to present the Jewish authorities as a collective group often in opposition to Jesus, rather than referring to the entire ethnic population. The syntax of the indirect statement introduced by 'that' (ὅτι) with the present indicative 'is' (ἐστίν) emphasizes the ongoing identity of Jesus as the healer, contrasting with the completed action of the healing itself.

translation: And for this reason the Jews were persecuting Jesus, because he was doing these things on a Sabbath.
notes: The sentence employs the causal conjunction οὖν (implied by the context of 'for this reason' or οὖν) combined with διά with the accusative (διὰ τοῦτο) to establish a clear causal link. The verb διώκω (to persecute, hunt, or pursue) is in the imperfect indicative active (ἠδίωκον), indicating repeated or continuous action in the past, which reflects the escalating hostility of the Jewish authorities toward Jesus. The use of the imperfect ἐποίει (he was doing) in the subordinate clause introduced by ὅτι (because) highlights the ongoing nature of the actions that triggered the persecution. The phrase ἐν σαββάτῳ (on a Sabbath) is crucial to the cultural context, as the Jewish leaders' opposition to Jesus often centered on his perceived violation of Sabbath regulations regarding healing and work. The sentence structure is straightforward, with the causal clause explaining the motive for the main action, a common feature in Johannine narrative to underscore theological conflict.

translation: But he answered them.
notes: The sentence employs the postpositive particle δέ (δέ) to mark a transition or contrast, a common feature in narrative discourse that connects this response to preceding dialogue. The verb ἀποκρίνομαι is in the aorist indicative middle voice (ἀπεκρίνατο), a form frequently used in koine Greek to denote the act of answering a question or responding to a statement. In this context, the middle voice emphasizes the subject's engagement in the response. The pronoun αὐτοῖς is dative plural, functioning as the indirect object of the verb, indicating the recipients of the answer. The article ὁ serves as the subject, referring to a male antecedent established in the immediate prior context. The syntax is straightforward subject-verb-object, with the conjunction δέ providing the necessary narrative flow.

translation: My Father is working until now, and I am working.
notes: The sentence features a parallel structure (isocolon) between the two clauses, emphasizing the continuity of the Father's action and the speaker's participation in it. The verb ἐργάζομαι (to work) is used in the present indicative in both clauses, with the first in the third person and the second in the first person, linked by the coordinating conjunction καί (and). The phrase ἕως ἄρτι (until now) functions as a temporal adverbial modifier for the first verb, indicating an action that began in the past and continues into the present moment. The use of the enclitic form καὶ (represented here as κα- before the vowel-initial pronoun ἐγώ) demonstrates standard elision before a following vowel. The syntax highlights a shared agency between the divine Father and the speaker, a theme often found in Johannine literature where the Son acts in perfect unity with the Father.

translation: For this reason the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because not only was he breaking the sabbath, but he was also calling God his own Father, making himself equal to God.
notes: The sentence employs a causal structure introduced by 'δια τοῦτο' (for this reason) followed by the explanatory 'ὅτι' (because). The intensifier 'μᾶλλον' (more/all the more) modifies 'ἐζήτουν' (they were seeking), indicating an escalation in the Jews' hostility. The clause following 'ὅτι' utilizes the 'οὐ μόνον... ἀλλὰ καί' (not only... but also) construction to emphasize the severity of Jesus' actions in the eyes of his opponents. The verb 'ἔλυεν' (he was loosing/breaking) is used in the context of the Sabbath, referring to the violation of its regulations. The phrase 'πατέρα ἴδιον ἐλεγεν' (he was calling his own Father) uses the adjective 'ἴδιον' (own/peculiar) to denote a unique relationship, which was perceived as blasphemy. The participle 'ποιῶν' (making) with the accusative 'ἴσον' (equal) and dative 'τῷ θεῷ' (to God) functions as a result or explanatory clause, clarifying the theological implication of calling God his own Father: self-elevation to the status of the deity.

translation: So Jesus answered and said to them.
notes: This sentence exemplifies a common narrative formula in Koine Greek, particularly in the Gospels, where two verbs are joined by 'kai' (and) to denote a sequence of closely related actions: 'apokrithē' (answered) followed by 'elegen' (was saying). The use of the imperfect 'elegen' alongside the aorist 'apokrithē' suggests that the 'answering' is a punctual event, while the 'saying' represents the ongoing content of that answer. The particle 'oun' (so/therefore) functions as a discourse marker, linking this response to the preceding dialogue or context. The dative plural 'autois' (to them) indicates the recipients of Jesus' speech, likely referring to the group with whom he is interacting. The structure is straightforward, with no complex rhetorical devices, but the repetition of 'and' (asyndeton is absent here, as 'kai' is present) emphasizes the immediacy of the response.

translation: Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of himself, unless he sees the Father doing it.
notes: The sentence opens with the emphatic repetition of the adverb ἀμήν (amen), a formulaic device in the Gospel of John used to introduce solemn, authoritative pronouncements. The verb λέγω is in the present indicative active, while the main verb of the subordinate clause, δύναται, is also present indicative middle, indicating general ability or capacity rather than a specific past or future event. The construction ὁ υἱὸς ποιεῖν ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ οὐδέν utilizes a negative clause where οὐδέν (nothing) serves as the object of the infinitive ποιεῖν, modified by the prepositional phrase ἀφ’ ἑαυτοῦ (from himself). The clause ἂν μή τι βλέπῃ τὸν πατέρα ποιοῦντα introduces a conditional restriction. Here, ἂν + the present subjunctive βλέπῃ forms a present general conditional, implying 'whenever he does not see' or 'unless he sees.' The phrase τὸν πατέρα ποιοῦντα features a present active participle agreeing with πατέρα, functioning as a complementary participle that describes the action of the Father which the Son observes. This syntactic structure highlights the theological dependence of the Son's actions on the Father's will, framed through the visual metaphor of 'seeing'.

translation: For whatever that one does, these things the Son also does likewise.
notes: This sentence features a conditional structure introduced by the particle 'γαρ' (for) combined with the subjunctive mood in the relative clause ('ποιῇ', from ποιέω, though the text provided shows ποιῇ which is a variant or OCR artifact for ποιῇ) and the modal particle 'ἄν'. The construction 'ὅ τι ἄν' (whatever... might) sets up a general condition. The main clause uses the present indicative ('ποιεῖ') to state a habitual or continuous action. The word order emphasizes the parallelism between 'that one' (referring to the Father) and 'the Son', linked by 'καί' (also) and 'ὁμοίως' (likewise/similarly). The phrase 'ταῦτα' (these things) acts as a neuter plural object, likely referring back to actions mentioned in the preceding context. The syntax highlights the theological concept of the Son acting in perfect unity and imitation of the Father's will.

translation: For the Father loves the Son and shows him all things that he himself does, and he will show him greater works than these, so that you may marvel.
notes: The sentence exhibits a clear progression of revelation through the verb δεικνύω (to show), moving from the present tense (shows) to the future (will show). The construction ἵνα with the present subjunctive (θαυμάζετε) indicates a purpose clause expressing the intended result of the Father's actions. The phrase πάντα δεικνυσιν αὐτῷ ἃ αὐτὸς ποιεῖ uses a relative clause (ἃ) to define the scope of what is shown, emphasizing the intimate knowledge and shared activity between Father and Son. The comparative structure μειζόνα τούτων (greater than these) creates a climactic escalation, suggesting that the future works will surpass the current signs in magnitude or significance. The use of αὐτὸς for emphasis (he himself) highlights the Son's agency in the actions being revealed. The second person plural subjunctive (υμεῖς θαυμάζετε) directly addresses the audience, inviting them into a state of wonder at the divine revelation.

translation: For just as the Father raises the dead and gives life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes.
notes: This sentence employs a classic comparative structure (ὥσπερ ... οὕτως, 'just as ... so also') to establish a theological parallel between the actions of the Father and the Son. The syntax highlights the Son's absolute authority by paralleling the Father's sovereign act of raising the dead. The verb ζωοποιεῖ ('gives life' or 'makes alive') appears twice, creating a subtle anaphora that reinforces the theme of divine life-giving power. The use of the relative pronoun οὓς ('whom') with the dative sense implied by the context of 'to whomever' emphasizes the personal and voluntary nature of the Son's action, contingent solely on his will (θέλει). The particle γάρ ('for') indicates that this statement serves as a causal explanation or justification for a preceding argument regarding judgment and authority.

translation: For the Father judges no one, but has committed all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son even as they honor the Father.
notes: This sentence employs a clear contrastive structure using the adversative conjunction 'ἀλλά' (but) to juxtapose divine inaction regarding judgment with the active delegation of that authority. The verb 'κρίνει' (judges) is negated by the double negative construction 'οὐδέ' (not even/none), emphasizing the absolute scope of the Father's abstention. The purpose clause introduced by 'ἵνα' (so that) takes the present subjunctive 'τιμῶσι' (may honor), indicating a continuous or habitual action required of the audience. The final clause, introduced by 'καθὼς' (just as/as), creates a parallelism between honoring the Son and honoring the Father. This parallelism is structurally reinforced by the repetition of the verb 'τιμῶσι' and the direct objects 'τὸν υἱὸν' and 'τὸν πατέρα', establishing a theological equivalence in the treatment of both figures. The text utilizes a balanced, rhythmic flow common in theological discourse to underscore the unity of honor due to both the Father and the Son.

translation: He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.
notes: This sentence exhibits a clear chiastic structure (A-B-C...C-B-A) in its thematic elements: honoring the Son, honoring the Father, and the Father's action of sending the Son. The syntax relies on a present active participle (τιμῶν, 'honoring') functioning as a substantive subject ('the one who honors'), modified by the negative adverb μή (μή τιμῶν). This is contrasted with the main verb in the indicative mood (τιμᾷ, 'he honors'), negated by the negative adverb οὐ (οὐ τιμᾷ). The participle πεμψάντα ('having sent') acts as an attributive adjective modifying 'Father' (πατέρα), with the accusative pronoun αὐτόν ('him') serving as its object. The sentence highlights the theological principle that rejection of the Son is intrinsically linked to rejection of the Sender, a common motif in Johannine literature where the Son is the exclusive revelation of the Father.

translation: Truly, truly, I say to you that whoever hears my word and believes the one who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment but has passed from death into life.
notes: The sentence opens with the emphatic repetition 'ἀμὴν ἀμὴν' (truly, truly), a distinctive formula used by Jesus in the Gospel of John to introduce statements of paramount importance. The subject of the main clause is a substantive participle phrase ('ὁ... ἀκούων καὶ πιστεύων'), where the definite article 'ὁ' nominalizes the participles 'hearing' and 'believing' to create the concept of 'the one who...'. The verb 'ἔχει' (has) is in the present indicative, indicating a current possession, while 'μεταβεβήκεν' (has passed) is a perfect indicative active, emphasizing the completed action with ongoing results. The text employs a clear antithesis (contrast) between 'death' (θάνατος) and 'life' (ζωή), and between 'coming into judgment' (εἰς κρίσιν ἔρχεται) and 'passing over' (μεταβεβήκεν). The prepositional phrases 'ἐκ... εἰς...' (from... into...) create a spatial metaphor for the transition of the believer's state.

translation: Truly, truly, I say to you that the hour is coming, and now it is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.
notes: The sentence opens with the emphatic double ἀμήν (amen), a formula used by Jesus in the Gospel of John to introduce statements of supreme importance or theological truth. The phrase 'the hour is coming, and now it is' (ἔρχεται ὥρα καὶ νῦν ἐστιν) utilizes a present tense verb (ἔρχεται) alongside a perfective sense of arrival ('now it is') to express the 'already/not yet' eschatological tension characteristic of Johannine theology: the end times are approaching but have already begun in the person of Jesus. The relative clause introduced by ὅτε (when) contains a prophetic promise involving the passive voice of hearing (ἀκούσουσιν) and a resultant state of life (ζήσουσιν). The syntax creates a causal chain: hearing the voice leads directly to life. The phrase 'voice of the Son of God' uses a genitive chain (φωνῆς τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ) which emphasizes the divine authority of the speaker whose voice brings resurrection. The use of the aorist participle ἀκούσαντες ('those who heard/having heard') as the subject of the future verb ζήσουσιν ('will live') highlights the decisive, completed act of hearing that results in eternal life.

translation: For just as the Father has life in himself, so also he has given to the Son to have life in himself.
notes: This sentence employs a classic 'just as... so also' (ὡςπερ... οὕτως) correlative structure, establishing a theological analogy between the Father's intrinsic possession of life and the Son's derived authority to possess it. The phrase 'in himself' (ἐν ἑαυτῷ) appears twice, emphasizing the self-existent nature of the Father and the delegated, yet inherent, life-giving power granted to the Son. The use of the dative case for the indirect object ('to the Son') combined with the infinitive of purpose ('to have') highlights the transfer of authority. The particle γάρ indicates that this statement serves as an explanation or justification for a preceding context regarding judgment or the nature of divine life. Stylistically, the parallelism between the two clauses creates a rhythmic balance typical of Johannine theological discourse.

translation: And he gave him the authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.
notes: The verb 'ἐξουσίαν ἔδωκεν' (gave authority) employs the accusative of the thing given, while the infinitive 'ποιεῖν' (to do/make) functions as an object complement, a construction common in Koine Greek to express the purpose or content of the authority granted. The phrase 'κρισίν ποιεῖν' is a specific idiom meaning 'to judge' or 'to execute judgment.' The clause introduced by 'ὅτι' (because) provides the theological justification for this authority. The title 'υἱὸς ἀνθρώπου' (Son of Man) is a significant messianic title derived from Daniel 7:13-14 and Ezekiel, often used by Jesus in the Gospels to refer to himself, emphasizing both his humanity and his divine, eschatological role as the judge of the world. The sentence structure juxtaposes the granting of power with the identity of the recipient, linking the authority directly to his unique status.

translation: Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, and those who have done good things will come forth to a resurrection of life, but those who have done evil things to a resurrection of judgment.
notes: This sentence employs a clear chiasmus in its final clause, contrasting 'those who have done good' (οἱ τὰ ἀγαθὰ ποιήσαντες) with 'those who have done evil' (οἱ τὰ φαῦλα πράξαντες), paired respectively with 'resurrection of life' (ἀνάστασιν ζωῆς) and 'resurrection of judgment' (ἀνάστασιν κρίσεως). The use of the aorist participles ποιήσαντες and πράξαντες highlights the completed nature of the actions that determine the outcome. The phrase 'the hour is coming' (ἔρχεται ὥρα) utilizes a present tense verb with future sense, a common feature in apocalyptic and prophetic discourse to denote an imminent certainty. The construction 'in the tombs' (ἐν τοῖς μνημείοις) uses the plural, emphasizing the universality of the dead subject to the coming event. The sentence structure moves from a negative imperative (μη θαυμαζετε) to a causal explanation (οτι) detailing the eschatological event.

translation: I am not able to do anything from myself.
notes: The sentence features the negative construction οὐ δύναμαι, where the adverb οὐ precedes the verb to negate the ability. The subject ἐγώ is explicitly stated for emphasis, a common feature in the Johannine style to highlight personal agency or lack thereof. The infinitive ποιεῖν functions as the object of the verb δύναμαι (a construction known as the complementary infinitive). The phrase ἀπ' ἐμαυτοῦ uses the preposition ἀπό with the genitive of the reflexive pronoun to denote origin or source, literally 'from myself.'
